newsitem.title: UK: EU opt-out now would be "terrible mistake" - Clarke.
newsitem.headline: EU opt-out now would be "terrible mistake" - Clarke.

text.p: Britain's pro-European finance minister Kenneth Clarke, at the centre of a row over monetary union, said the government would be making a "terrible mistake" if it decided now to opt out of a single European currency.

Clarke told Thursday's Times newspaper that deciding to opt out of a planned single European currency now "would be ruling out the possibility of making a judgment that could have a vital effect on jobs and prosperity some time in the future."
On Wednesday, Clarke had sought to play down a remark by foreign minister Malcolm Rifkind that Britain was "on balance hostile" to the European Union's planned single currency.
But Rifkind said he had fully intended the comment, which was seen as a departure from a carefully-brokered Cabinet agreement of studied neutrality on monetary union.
Clarke insisted the government's "wait and see" policy was intact.
"We remain open-minded on the subject," he told the Times. He said he believed there could be "considerable advantages" for Britain in joining a succesful monetary union.
But Clarke is sceptical of the planned timetable for union, set to begin on January 1, 1999. He says he believes the start-date will have to be delayed.
The Conservative government's opponents seized on the rift between Rifkind and Clarke with glee.
"You have got government ministers at sixes and sevens...it is a quite extraordinary situation," said opposition Labour leader Tony Blair.
"The government can't sustain a position on Europe for a week," said Paddy Ashdown, leader of the minority Liberal Democrats, Britain's most pro-European party.
Rifkind made his remarks in Bonn ahead of a speech on Britain's attitude to the European Union in which he emphasised the need to guard against centralisation of power to Brussels.

The single currency is a tricky issue for Major because of the conflict within his party between ministers like Clarke who believe Britain should join provided it is properly set up and MPs who have set their face completely against it and distrust anything that emanates from Brussels.

A government line had appeared agreed when Rifkind and Clarke emerged from a cabinet meeting last month to declare that while Britain would keeping its options open, it was unlikely to join up if the currency went ahead as planned in 1999.
Some commentators saw Rifkind's remarks as a bid for support from Conservative Eurosceptics in case he decides to stand in a possible party leadership race.
Prime Minister John Major must call an election by May and with his party lagging Labour by around 20 points in opinion polls, he looks unlikely to regain power.
Following Rifkind's remark and Clarke's dismissal of it, Major was left to attempt to paper over the differences.
He told journalists the government would need to be persuaded that it was "positively beneficial" to join a single currency before it would do so.
"We would need to be persuaded that it was better. We are not so persuaded at the moment," he said.
